content.title: About
content.content: Cilantro (Coriandrum sativum) is an annual herb widely used as a fresh garnish in cooking. Its bright‑green leaves have a distinctive citrusy aroma and are common in Asian, Latin American, and Mediterranean dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cilantro is known as coriander when referring to its seeds, and as cilantro when referring to the leaves.
In some cuisines the herb is added at the end of cooking to preserve its fresh flavor.
A genetic variation causes a portion of the population to perceive cilantro’s taste as soapy.
The seeds are used as a spice, while the leaves are used fresh.
Cilantro can be easily grown at home in pots.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: The leaves contain vitamin C, quercetin, and other polyphenols that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Essential oils and dietary fiber stimulate bile production and improve intestinal motility.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Cilantro provides vitamin B6 and folate, important for metabolism and DNA synthesis.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A generous serving of cilantro adds minimal calories, making it suitable for weight‑conscious diets.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: The herb supplies potassium, magnesium, and iron, supporting heart function and blood health.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cilantro, such as skin itching or swelling.

items.title: Microbial contamination
items.content: Raw leafy greens can be contaminated with bacteria (e.g., E. coli); thorough washing before use is recommended.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Cilantro may enhance the effects of anticoagulant medications, so people on such drugs should consult a healthcare professional.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use cilantro fresh in salads, salsas, soups, marinades, and as a garnish for fish, meat, and rice dishes. It can be blended into smoothies or sauces. For maximum flavor, sprinkle chopped leaves over finished dishes just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cilantro in the refrigerator wrapped in a slightly damp paper towel inside a sealed bag. It stays fresh for 5–7 days. For longer storage, freeze the leaves in ice‑cube trays with a little water.
